channel.title: Science News
channel.description: Aggregated headlines linking to original publishers

item.title: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
item.description: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

item.title: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining
item.description: Scientists have discovered that gut bacteria can feed on the protective mucus lining your intestines, producing potentially harmful compounds, but fiber helps keep this activity in check. Overlooked proteins in plant foods also help shift gut bacteria toward producing beneficial substances, revealing a surprising new reason plant-based diets may be good for you.

item.title: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
item.description: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality.

item.title: CHAPEA Mission 2 Crew Reflects After 378 Days on Simulated Mars
item.description: After 378 days without windows, the sounds of the outside world, or real-time calls with family and friends, four research volunteers stepped out of NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, completing the agency’s second yearlong Mars surface simulation. Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer, and Matthew Montgomery entered the roughly 1,700-square-foot, 3D-printed habitat at […]

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
item.description: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.

item.title: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
item.description: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

item.title: Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space
item.description: For the first time, a robot has autonomously built part of a structure in space, demonstrating a breakthrough that could fundamentally change space exploration. The technology could one day allow scientists to construct enormous telescopes, communications antennas, and solar power stations in orbit, far beyond the size limits of today's rockets.

item.title: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
item.description: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

item.title: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
item.description: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.

item.title: Ozone Hole Reaches Its 2026 Maximum
item.description: The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but it was not as deep as other large holes on record.

item.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
item.description: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

item.title: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a buildup of a protein called Miro1 may be a hidden driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes, with preclinical experiments showing that removing it restores the muscles’ response to insulin. Exercise was also found to lower Miro1 levels in people with diabetes, revealing a potential new pathway for treating the disease.

item.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

item.title: The super El Niño is more than a climate shock – it’s a health one, too
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03628-5 Food shortages and disease outbreaks are to be expected and need to be addressed together.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03626-7 The theoretical physicist unpacks the need for more humility in science and whether artificial intelligence could ever become conscious.

item.title: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03631-w Scientists say governments must commit to carbon dioxide removal if world is to bring temperatures back down to safer limits.

item.title: AI has transformed maths — this is how we got here
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03627-6 The story of how maths came to run the world, and created the artificial-intelligence models that might surpass human mathematicians.

item.title: How academic freedom is changing around the world — by the numbers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02998-0 Nature reports on five countries where academic freedom either plummeted or soared in recent years.

item.title: Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered
item.description: Researchers have discovered a stunning new species of tiny orange-patterned fish in the Brazilian Amazon, but its survival may already be at risk. Named Laimosemion laranja, the brilliantly colored killifish measures less than three centimeters long and was found in just three small forest pools. Its extremely limited habitat is threatened by mining, deforestation, pollution, and expanding development.

item.title: Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy
item.description: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a powerful new cancer therapy that remains inactive until it reaches the brain, where it switches on to attack deadly tumors. The engineered immune cells, called B-SYNC CAR-T cells, completely eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that is almost always fatal within a year, in two mouse models.

item.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
item.description: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

item.title: Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy
item.description: More than a century after Einstein revolutionized our understanding of gravity, scientists have uncovered a surprising new phenomenon hidden within his equations. Researchers at Columbia University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez have identified a theoretical process called "gravitational reconnection," in which structures within gravitational fields can break apart and reconnect, transferring energy into matter.

item.title: NASA Announces $1 Million to Students for Moon Base Challenge
item.description: On Sunday, NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. As part of a Golden Age of Science, the competition invites student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools to contribute designs for the Moon Base. “We’re […]

item.title: A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut
item.description: Scientists have discovered that fasting for just 24 hours increases a beneficial gut bacterium that helps the intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could pave the way for new treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.

item.title: MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body
item.description: MIT scientists have developed nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells directly inside the body to attack cancer and harmful immune cells, eliminating tumors and reversing liver damage in mouse experiments. The breakthrough could make powerful immune therapies dramatically simpler and less expensive while opening new possibilities for treating cancer and autoimmune diseases.

item.title: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch
item.description: A nuclear explosion might save Earth from a deadly asteroid, but new research suggests that hitting the wrong side could make the difference between success and disaster. Scientists found that an asteroid's irregular shape can dramatically affect how it responds to an X-ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying nearly fivefold depending on the angle.

item.title: Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
item.description: A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

item.title: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
item.description: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

item.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
item.description: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

item.title: Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot
item.description: Scientists have created record-breaking X-ray flashes lasting just 300 attoseconds, concentrating enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot. The breakthrough could unlock a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.

item.title: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that those who received a high-dose influenza vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's, compared with a 40% reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction
item.description: A study of more than 17,700 US adults found that people who use cannabis in multiple forms have dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms than those who stick primarily to one method. Nearly 67% of those who used almost every form met criteria for cannabis use disorder, compared with just 15% of people who mainly consumed edibles.

item.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
item.description: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

item.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.

item.title: NASA Awards Moon Base Transportation, Technology, Science Projects
item.description: NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities. The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on […]

item.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
item.description: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight. Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. The next generation […]

item.title: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
item.description: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

item.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
item.description: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

item.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
item.description: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

item.title: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
item.description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view.

item.title: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.

item.title: A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease
item.description: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia, a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system, by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, although clinical trials are still needed to establish its effectiveness in patients.

item.title: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
item.description: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.

item.title: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
item.description: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds.

item.title: M30’s Sparkling Stars

The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier, who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about […]

item.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

item.title: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins
item.description: A study of nearly 5,800 adults found that heart scans measuring calcium buildup in the arteries led to the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, despite recommending statins to far fewer patients. Surprisingly, patients advised to take statins based on their scans were nearly three times as likely to stick with their medication, raising intriguing questions about how doctors should identify and treat heart disease risk.

item.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
item.description: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

item.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
item.description: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

item.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
item.description: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

item.title: For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise
item.description: Full-fat dairy may not be the health villain it has long been portrayed as, according to a new study finding that three daily servings did not worsen weight, cholesterol, or insulin resistance over 12 weeks. Researchers also observed improvements in blood pressure and nutrient intake, raising questions about longstanding recommendations to choose low-fat dairy.

item.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

item.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.

item.title: Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
item.description: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.

item.title: A clever molecular trick unlocks previously impossible properties in glass
item.description: Scientists have discovered how to reprogram the internal structure of glass using a special molecule that rearranges chemical bonds while lowering the melting temperature. The breakthrough could unlock entirely new glass materials with precisely controlled magnetic and optical properties, opening possibilities for advanced electronics, sensors, and other technologies.

item.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution
item.description: A groundbreaking discovery is rewriting the story of human evolution, revealing that an ancient human species once thought to be an evolutionary dead end may have left genetic traces in people alive today. By extracting proteins from 400,000-year-old Homo erectus teeth discovered in China, scientists uncovered evidence suggesting that these early humans interbred with Denisovans, another mysterious ancient human group. That genetic connection may have eventually reached modern populations in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and other parts of Southeast Asia.

item.title: Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel
item.description: Scientists have developed a revolutionary gel that could regrow lost tooth enamel by harnessing minerals naturally found in saliva, potentially overcoming one of dentistry’s biggest limitations. The regenerated enamel behaves much like healthy enamel, raising hopes for a simple treatment that could repair damaged teeth, prevent decay, and reduce sensitivity.

item.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
item.description: Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03568-0 Policies designed to keep women in the workforce could be entrenching gendered parenting roles.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03596-w The manual toothbrush cleans by generating a bacteria-killing electrical charge. Plus, what ‘historic’ US mid-term results mean for science and a genetics lab run by AI-powered robots.

item.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
item.description: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

item.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
item.description: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

item.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
item.description: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.

item.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
item.description: MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.

item.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
item.description: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

item.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
item.description: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

item.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

item.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
item.description: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.

item.title: Parkinson’s: beyond the brain
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03173-1 Parkinson’s disease might develop in the gut before reaching the brain, and the environment could have a crucial role in triggering the disease.

item.title: AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03552-8 Self-driving lab in China requires only a simple prompt to encode messages in DNA and read them out.

item.title: The oracle of the second quadrant
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03369-5 It all adds up.

item.title: X-ray stopwatch can measure durations of just attoseconds
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03423-2 The duration of short ångström-wavelength X-ray pulses, which lasted merely 170 attoseconds, has finally been measured accurately. The optical system designed for precision pulse duration metrology can be used as a ‘stopwatch’ to measure the rapid motion of electrons inside atoms and molecules, too.

item.title: Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03343-1 Some countries are introducing sweeping social-media bans for young people, but the impact of screen time is still under investigation.

item.title: ‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03579-x Researchers hope that US lawmakers will push back against the Trump administration’s science policies — but there are limits to what Congress can do.

item.title: How a once-controversial idea is advancing understanding of Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03169-x The disease is thought to be divided into two subtypes, depending on where it originates in the body — the gut or the brain.

item.title: Rise of Germanic and Celtic languages is written in ancient DNA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03581-3 Thousands of genome sequences identify human migrations that might have spread early forms of these tongues around Europe.

item.title: AI agents enter the ‘wet lab’
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03270-1 An AI system coordinates laboratory instruments to conduct multi-step molecular-biology experiments with limited human intervention.

item.title: How the brain protects itself from Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03171-3 Brains are resilient. Harnessing their self-protective mechanisms might help to prevent or slow the progression of this neurodegenerative condition.

item.title: Daily briefing: See a tardigrade shed its skin
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03593-z Enjoy the month’s best science images. Plus, an outbreak of anthrax in African hippos and the places where biodiversity drops after humans leave.

item.title: Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03167-z Most Parkinson’s therapies aim to reduce the motor-control symptoms that the disease triggers. But stem-cell transplants in the brain could alter the disease at a more fundamental level.

item.title: Progress accelerates in Parkinson’s treatments
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03165-1 Researchers are reporting encouraging results for a disease that affects millions of people worldwide.

item.title: Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03544-8 It might seem counterproductive to put more people in nature, but sometimes human activity nurtures biodiversity.

item.title: See a tardigrade shed its skin — October’s best science images
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03563-5 The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

item.title: Fruit, flies and getting frisky: how food odours trigger sexual arousal
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03271-0 Males of a Drosophila species that thrives on a particular fruit need the smell of food to begin courtship. This environmental cue acts on defined mating circuits in the brain.

item.title: Six highlights from Parkinson’s disease research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03172-2 Targeting a new network, addressing gait issues and other advances from recent studies.

item.title: Cutting-edge technique uncovers how the spine’s shock absorbers bear load
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03264-z An exciting imaging approach reveals how discs of soft tissue in the spine respond to compressive force at the micrometre and nanometre scales.

item.title: Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03566-2 A clinical trial in three people tested a combination of gene-laden viruses and a drug.

item.title: A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03269-8 The process of making protein from RNA can go awry in cancer cells. This malfunction might be harnessed to create an effective gene-therapy tool that targets tumours.

item.title: Faint exoplanets detected using computational approach to remove glare from stars
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03295-6 An image-processing framework for detecting exoplanets directly has been developed. The technique overcomes the telescope-stability barrier that has limited previous methods, reveals fainter exoplanets than other approaches can detect and could make imaging exo-Earths easier for future observatories.

item.title: People’s social networks can be unintentionally reshaped during randomized interventions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03267-w A re-examination of a randomized controlled trial for a health-advice intervention reveals ripple effects and altered relationships in communities in rural Honduras.

item.title: Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03168-y Neuroscientists are developing a new type of brain implant that will decode every movement and symptom of people with this neurodegenerative condition, seeking better ways to ease symptoms.

item.title: Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03580-4 The latest cases, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, come as the country grapples with ongoing Ebola and cholera outbreaks.

item.title: When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03505-1 For decades, conservation has worried about the risks of too many people. In some places, depopulation is the real threat.

item.title: Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03170-4 Researchers and advocates point to pollutants as a trigger for the neurodegenerative condition.

item.title: Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03166-0 After decades of work, researchers have begun trialling transplants of dopamine neurons into people with the neurodegenerative disease — with early signs of success.

item.title: Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03413-4 Scientists have yet to reveal how the human brain produces the subjective experience we perceive as consciousness, but research has pushed the field in exciting directions.

item.title: Infrared image detectors grown directly on read-out chips
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03420-5 A film of lead sulfide — an infrared-sensitive semiconductor — has been grown directly on a circuit that can read out the material’s electrical signal through an approach called monolithic in situ integration. This brings material growth and electronic integration together into a single step. The resulting image sensor shows high sensitivity for infrared wavelengths.

item.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8 A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.

item.title: Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11133-y Recent progress in photovoltaics has been investigated to translate state-of-the-art cells in the laboratory into deployable products suited to real indoor conditions, focusing on wide-bandgap absorbers, reduced non-radiative voltage losses and reshaping module design.

item.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10956-z Using high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.

item.title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11225-9 A programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator is used to explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits, revealing prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting.

item.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11209-9 In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.

item.title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11228-6 AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

item.title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11148-5 The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.

item.title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11238-4 Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.

item.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11177-0 Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

item.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11212-0 A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis.

item.title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11226-8 Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

item.title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11245-5 Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.

item.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11200-4 Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells.

item.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11198-9 Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories.

item.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11224-w Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

item.title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5 A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours.

item.title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11248-2 Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus.

item.title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9 Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

item.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11236-6 Gene network analysis shows how mutations in diverse genes associated with autism spectrum disorder can converge to exert shared effects, with X-linked transcription factor ZFX emerging as a key protective factor in the female brain.

item.title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5 Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.

item.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

item.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
item.description: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

item.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
item.description: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

item.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
item.description: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours.
